picks.title: Being real
picks.summary:
In this Wednesday Night Dharma Talk, Frank Ostaseski traces what he learned sitting at the bedside of thousands of dying people: “to sit next to people and not mess with them. Not try and help them have some experience, or meet someone else’s agenda, including their own. Just sit with them.” That same quality of presence, he suggests, is what it means to ‘be real’ — an alignment with reality…
Source
picks.reason: Talk on presence with dying, emphasizing reality and being real, resonant with Taoist values.

picks.title: Choro Antonaccio : Offerings to the Buddhas
picks.summary:
Dharma Talk by Zen priest Choro Antonaccio.Choro is the Abiding Teacher of Austin Zen Center. She began formal Zen practice in 1999 at Chapel Hill Zen Center, where she was lay and priest ordained by Josho Pat Phelan Roshi. Choro also trained at Tassajara, Green Gulch Farm, and City Center. She is a Dharma Heir of Abbot Gaelyn.

picks.title: Grace in Prison
picks.summary:
In this Wednesday Night Dharma Talk, Sensei Dainin describes bringing Roshi Joan’s G.R.A.C.E. compassion training into New Mexico’s prison system. Working previously with the correctional cadets, and now with men who are incarcerated, Dainin names how the system pushes both groups into opposition, each side dehumanizing the other by default. Looking for guidance on how to serve well in that…
Source
picks.reason: Discusses compassion training in prison, ethical and spiritual reflection in Zen context.

picks.title: Four Friendly Facts by Kanshin Allison Tait
picks.summary: This Dharma talk explores the Four Noble Truths through Robert Thurman’s playful framing of the “Four Friendly Fun Facts.” Looking at suffering as something to understand rather than escape, the talk considers how self-centeredness creates alienation, how compassion reconnects us with others, and how the Eightfold Path offers a practical way to work with our lives as they actually are. Along the way, it touches on impermanence, Tonglen practice, and approaching Buddhist practice as an ongoing experiment in wisdom and compassion.Books mentioned: Wisdom Is Bliss: Four Friendly Fun Facts That Can
picks.reason: Explores suffering, compassion, and impermanence through Buddhist teachings, close to Taoist concerns.
